issues.legal_issue: A custom governing inheritance must be proved unless repeated judicial recognition has made it entitled to judicial notice, and the alleged custom preferring collaterals over a sister in succession to non-ancestral property had not reached that status.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a sister's claim to her brother's non-ancestral property against a collateral relative.
The collateral relied on paragraph 24 of Rattigan's Digest for the asserted custom excluding sisters in favour of collaterals.
The reported decisions were divided on whether that custom existed, and decisions in the preceding ten years uniformly rejected the view in the Digest.
issues.conclusion: The alleged custom could not be judicially noticed on the authority of the Digest alone and required proof in the case; customs, whether described as general or otherwise, ordinarily require proof unless repeated recognition by courts entitles them to judicial notice.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 48 and 57(1) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, custom may be proved, but proof is unnecessary where courts can take judicial notice of it. A custom becomes entitled to judicial notice when it has been repeatedly brought to the courts' attention and recognised as part of the law. The Court relied on Raja Rama Rao v. Raja of Pittapur for that threshold, and on Daya Ram v. Sohel Singh and Abdul Hussein Khan v. Bibi Sona Dero for the ordinary burden on the party asserting a custom. It also observed that Rattigan's Digest, though highly authoritative, did not establish judicial recognition in the face of conflicting decisions.

rule.if: inheritance_custom_dispute and non_ancestral_property and conflicting_court_decisions and not repeated_court_recognition

predicates.inheritance_custom_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to property under an asserted customary rule of inheritance.
predicates.non_ancestral_property: The disputed property is not ancestral property of the deceased owner.
predicates.conflicting_court_decisions: Earlier courts have reached conflicting conclusions about whether the asserted custom exists.
predicates.repeated_court_recognition: Courts have repeatedly recognised the asserted custom as a rule of law.

issues.definition: When an inheritance custom concerning non-ancestral property is disputed and prior decisions conflict without repeated judicial recognition, the custom must be proved in the case.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant's description of her asserted entitlement as a special custom does not admit that an opposing party's alleged general custom exists or define its terms.
material_facts: The sister's plaint relied on a custom described as a special custom that gave her a preferential right to inherit.
The collateral argued that the sister's reference to a special custom admitted the existence of the general custom he asserted.
issues.conclusion: The sister's pleading did not amount to an admission of the alleged general custom or of its terms.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the pleading in context: asserting a special custom in favour of the claimant does not establish or admit a different custom relied on by the opponent. The party asserting the opponent's custom remains responsible for proving it.

predicates.inheritance_custom_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to property under asserted customary rules of inheritance.
predicates.claimant_pleads_special_custom: The claimant relies in the pleading on a custom described as special to a group, locality, or family.
predicates.opponent_relies_on_general_custom: The opposing party relies on a different custom said to apply generally.

issues.definition: In an inheritance custom dispute, a claimant's pleading of a special custom does not itself admit the existence or terms of the opponent's alleged general custom.

issues.legal_issue: A sister may establish a local custom entitling her to inherit her brother's non-ancestral property ahead of collaterals through relevant instances of such succession, while entries that concern only ancestral property do not prove a contrary rule for non-ancestral property.
material_facts: The parties belonged to the same agriculturist Jat sub-caste and village, and the property was not ancestral.
The sister relied on settlement records showing sisters or sisters' sons succeeding to property in the village despite the presence of collaterals.

The collateral relied on Riwaji-i-am entries that did not show that their answers concerned non-ancestral property; the recorded instances did not establish exclusion of a sister from non-ancestral property in the presence of collaterals.
The High Court accepted the sister's evidence, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disagree.
issues.conclusion: The sister proved a custom entitling her to succeed in preference to the collateral relatives.
issues.legal_principle: The party relying on a custom must prove it. Riwaji-i-am entries are ordinarily treated as referring to succession to ancestral property unless the entry or its context shows otherwise. The Court relied on the rule stated in Mst. Hurmate v. Hoshiaru concerning the scope of such entries, and assessed the local settlement records as evidence of the custom asserted for non-ancestral property.

rule.if: inheritance_custom_dispute and non_ancestral_property and local_sister_succession_instances and contrary_entries_not_shown_to_cover_non_ancestral_property

predicates.inheritance_custom_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to property under asserted customary rules of inheritance.
predicates.non_ancestral_property: The disputed property is not ancestral property of the deceased owner.
predicates.local_sister_succession_instances: Records from the relevant community or locality show sisters or their descendants succeeding to property despite the presence of collaterals.
predicates.contrary_entries_not_shown_to_cover_non_: Entries relied on to exclude sisters are not shown by their wording or context to address succession to non-ancestral property.

issues.definition: Where the property is non-ancestral, local records show sisters succeeding despite collaterals, and contrary entries are not shown to concern non-ancestral property, the sister's asserted preferential custom is established.

issues.legal_issue: When neither party establishes a custom governing succession, the parties' personal law supplies the rule of decision even if the claimant pleaded custom, and under the applicable Hindu law a sister inherits ahead of collaterals.
material_facts: The sister pleaded a customary basis for her claim, but the Court held that her claim could also succeed under the parties' personal law if her custom were not established.
The collateral's alleged custom preferring collaterals was not proved.
The parties were Sikhs to whom Hindu law applied, and the Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929, made a sister an heir ahead of collaterals.
The collateral did not dispute that the sister would take under Hindu law if that law applied.
issues.conclusion: Even if the sister had not proved her custom, she was entitled to succeed under the parties' Hindu personal law because the collateral had not proved a custom defeating that entitlement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Punjab Laws Act, 1872, makes applicable custom the first rule of decision in succession matters and, where no applicable custom is established, the parties' personal law. The Court relied on Daya Ram v. Sohel Singh, whose approach was approved in Abdul Hussein Khan v. Bibi Sona Dero, and on Mst. Fatima Bibi v. Shah Nawaz for allowing a claimant who pleaded custom to rely on personal law when custom was not established. Under the Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929, a sister was entitled ahead of collaterals.

rule.if: succession_dispute and hindu_personal_law_applies and sister_claims_against_collateral and opponent_custom_not_proved

predicates.succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns who inherits property from a deceased person.
predicates.hindu_personal_law_applies: The parties are governed by Hindu personal law for succession.
predicates.sister_claims_against_collateral: A sister claims the deceased person's property against a collateral relative.
predicates.opponent_custom_not_proved: The opposing party has not proved a custom that would displace the personal-law succession rule.

issues.definition: In a succession dispute governed by Hindu personal law, a sister claiming against a collateral inherits ahead of the collateral when the opposing party has not proved a contrary custom.
